judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1042. It would have ended the automatic life sentence for second-degree murder. New sentences would carry a minimum of at least 35 years, with life without parole only in listed cases, such as killing a police officer. People already serving life for second-degree murder could be paroled after 35 years, or after 20 years once they turn 70, with some exceptions. The bill also let prisoners earn credit toward a shorter minimum sentence for finishing job training and school programs. The Pennsylvania House passed the final version 102-100. As of August 2026 the bill had not become law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1062. It would have created a statewide registry, run by the state community and economic development department or a contractor it hires, listing owners whose serious property maintenance code violations stayed unfixed for a year. Municipalities and state agencies could use the registry when deciding on permits and licenses, and a listed owner could be fined $1,000 for each serious violation. The Pennsylvania House passed it 125-78. As of August 2026 the Senate had not voted on it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1396, a broad rewrite of the Pennsylvania Election Code. It would have created in-person early voting in every county, running from the 11th day before an election through the Sunday before election day. Every county would have to provide at least two ballot drop boxes and tell the state where they are at least 65 days before an election. A missing handwritten date or secrecy envelope would no longer void a mail ballot, and voters would get a chance to fix an unsigned one. Counties could begin processing mail ballots a week early, and election workers would be paid at least $175 per election. It would also have made citizen-requested recounts harder, raising the filing deposit from $50 to $850. The Pennsylvania House passed it 102-101. As of August 2026 the Senate had not voted on it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1706. It would have made the education department, working with the health and human services departments, publish guidance for students, parents and coaches on the warning signs of mental health trouble. Schools would have to tell families twice a year what mental health services are available. A school would have to refer a student to its student assistance program within 14 days if the student is habitually truant, shows a marked change in behavior, or suddenly stops attending an activity without explanation. Coaches at PIAA member schools would need mental health training starting in 2027-28. The Pennsylvania House passed it 107-94. As of August 2026 the Senate had not voted on it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2189. It would have raised Pennsylvania's minimum wage above the $7.25 federal floor: $11 an hour in 2027, $13 in 2028 and $15 in 2029, with yearly cost-of-living increases after that. Counties could set a higher rate, up to $15, starting in 2027. The state rate has been stuck at $7.15 since 2007. The Pennsylvania House passed it 104-95. As of August 2026 the Senate had not voted on it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 273. It also created a state grant program, up to $100,000 a town with matching funds, to help towns with no code enforcement start one. Penalty money would feed a fund paying for demolition, cleanup and repair of blighted property. The Pennsylvania House passed it 110-93. As of August 2026 the Senate had not voted on it.

The Pennsylvania House passed it 126-76. As of August 2026 the Senate had not voted on it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1042. It would have ended the automatic life sentence for second-degree murder, setting a minimum of at least 35 years instead, with life without parole only on specific aggravating findings. judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1400. Second-degree murder, a death caused during another serious crime, now carries an automatic life sentence. For offenders aged 18 or older the bill would have replaced that with a court-set minimum of at least 35 years and a maximum of up to life, so parole becomes possible. Courts could still impose life without parole in listed cases, such as a police-officer or child victim. People already serving life for second-degree murder could be paroled after 35 years, or at age 70 after 20 years. The Pennsylvania Senate passed it 30-20. As of August 2026 the House had not voted on it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 908. The prevailing wage law sets minimum pay on public construction jobs. This bill would have extended it to custom fabrication, meaning nonstandard parts made off site for a public project. It would also have removed three things from coverage: rehabilitating residential property with fewer than eight units, school safety work costing up to $50,000, and HVAC duct cleaning. The Pennsylvania Senate passed it 37-13. As of August 2026 the House had not voted on it.
